Half-life gives an estimate of how long half of a dose of labeled vitamin E remains in the plasma. The apparent half-life of RRR-a-
tocopherol in plasma of normal subjects is approximately 48 h, while that of SRR-a-tocopherol or g-tocopherol are only 15 h and
the tocotrienols are less than 4 h. More recent estimates suggest that the RRR-a-tocopherol half-life is 30–34 h (Mah et al., 2015;
Traber et al., 2019b). a-Tocopherol half-life is slowed in persons with hyperlipidemia, likely because lipoprotein catabolism is
slowed. Additionally, bioavailability is less in persons with metabolic syndrome or with fatty liver disease, which may exacerbate
oxidative stress associated with the increased inﬂammation in these disorders.
Vitamin E catabolism
a-TTP is the body’s key to maintaining plasma a-tocopherol concentrations, but the xenobiotic catabolism of non-a-tocopherol
vitamin E forms and “excess” a-tocopherol serves to increase their excretion and thus decrease their concentrations. Cytochrome
P450 4F2 (CYP4F2) initiates vitamin E catabolism by omega-hydroxylation of the sidechain to form the long chain, 130-hydroxy
(130-OH) catabolite (Sontag and Parker, 2002, 2007). The 130-OH catabolite undergoes u-oxidation to form the 130-carboxy (130-
